analysis.one_liner: Creates ethics advisors and an investigator with subpoena power inside the Supreme Court.
analysis.headline: Introduced February 25, 2026 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, the bill has had no hearings, markup, or vote since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set up two offices inside the Supreme Court: one to give justices advice on ethics rules like gifts, financial disclosure, and when to step aside from cases, and one to investigate ethics complaints against justices, with the power to compel witnesses and documents. Investigative findings would go to the Chief Justice or, if he is the subject, the most senior other justice, and to congressional committees. The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people get a formal channel for checking Supreme Court justices, who currently face no independent ethics investigation mechanism, and Congress gets annual data on how often justices seek ethics advice and whether they follow it.

how_it_helps.text: The bill creates an Office of Ethics Counsel to advise justices and their spouses on financial disclosure, gifts, political activity, conflicts and recusal, and requires justices to take biennial ethics training.

It creates an Office of Investigative Counsel to review ethics complaints against justices and their families' conduct, with subpoena power backed by contempt of court for anyone who refuses to comply.

The investigative office must report findings and recommendations to the Chief Justice (or, for complaints about the Chief Justice himself, to the most senior associate justice), to congressional Judiciary and oversight committees within 10 days, and to the Attorney General if it finds reason to believe federal criminal law was broken.
The ethics office must give the House and Senate Judiciary Committees an annual report on how much advice was sought, what topics it covered, and how often advice was not followed.

analysis.who_pays: Supreme Court justices would lose their near-total control over policing their own conduct, and anyone seeking to influence them through gifts or hospitality would face formal advice and possible investigation. Taxpayers fund the new offices' staff.

drawbacks.text: Only congressional leaders and Judiciary Committee chairs can file a complaint — ordinary citizens, parties, and watchdog groups cannot — and the bill's text says the Chief Justice 'is authorized to establish' the offices, so even its core machinery is framed as optional.

The Chief Justice appoints the counsels and can fire the chief counsel only 'for cause,' and he decides at his sole discretion whether any investigative report becomes public, so enforcement stays largely inside the Court it polices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would create real investigative machinery, including subpoena power and mandatory reports to Congress, where none exists now. But it is a modest design: the Chief Justice hires the enforcers, complaints must come from congressional leaders, and the Chief Justice decides what the public sees. It is a step toward accountability, not independent enforcement.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice in the Senate and referred to the Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and nothing has happened to it since.

narrative.text: Senator Cory Booker introduced the bill on February 25, 2026, joined by five Democratic cosponsors: Blumenthal, Hirono, Padilla, Schiff, and Welch.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary.
No further action — no hearing, markup, vote, or floor scheduling — appears in the bill's action history.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill went nowhere, Supreme Court justices keep policing their own ethics and no outside investigation mechanism exists. The status quo benefits the justices and anyone whose influence on them is never examined.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Did not schedule the bill for a hearing or markup after it was referred to his committee; the bill has sat without action since February 25, 2026.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor is a Senate Democrat (6 of the 47 Democratic-caucus members), and Republicans, who hold 55 Senate seats and chair the Judiciary Committee, have taken no action on it.

industries.note: The justices would become subject, for the first time, to formal ethics advice, mandatory training, and an investigative office that can subpoena records about their conduct. Their interest in preserving self-policing runs against the public's interest in an accountable highest court.
People who provide justices with gifts, hospitality, or paid engagements would face formal guidance and potential investigation, raising the cost of influence that currently draws little scrutiny.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding 55 Senate seats and chairing the Judiciary Committee, and no hearing or markup scheduled more than weeks after referral, the bill is unlikely to advance this session; the realistic path is that it sits in committee unless it picks up bipartisan support.
